media.title: Reporter's Notebook
media.description:
A. TOOL TITLE
- Reporter's Notebook
B. TOOL INFO
- Tool ID: M1.S1.T1.C2.2D1
- Tool type: Exploration
- Textbook source: Chapter 15 Data Through Pictures, the opening topic Child TV Reporter: the notebook of 35 answers and the table with the rows 1/2 hour, 1 hour, 1 1/2 hour, 2 hours and More than 2 hours; counts 9, 13, 7, 3 and 3 read off the notebook picture (developer only). The practice notebooks of 8, 9 and 10 answers are practice values.
C. LEARNING OBJECTIVE
- The student sees that a crowd of answers becomes a table when every answer goes once into the row where it belongs, and that the counts of all the rows add up to the number of answers.
- Out of scope: "more than" and "less than" questions on a finished table, the four questions about the table (they follow the concept video), pictographs and bar graphs.
D. TOOL DESCRIPTION
1. Opening Screen
- A reporter's wooden desk seen from above, as a photo. An open spiral notebook with blue ruled lines is the largest thing on the stage. On it are 8 hand-drawn round faces, each with a white speech bubble about a thumb-width wide: 2 hr, 1 hr, 3 hr, 1 hr, 2 hr, 1 hr, 3 hr, 1 hr.
- Beside it a clipboard holds a table with the headings "No. of Hours Spent Watching TV" and "No. of Children" and three empty rows, "1 hour", "2 hours", "3 hours", each with a count box showing 0.
- Instruction line: "Every answer goes in the row where it belongs."
- The first bubble (1 hr) glows. The child is invited to tap it.
2. Scene and Objects
- Samaira (microphone) and Kabir (pen) are small flat drawings in the top-left corner, about a tenth of the stage height. They do not move or speak.
- Faces are flat pen-and-ink children, spread out so no bubble covers another. Bubble: white with a blue outline, the answer in dark handwriting-style type, readable on a tablet. A sorted bubble leaves a pale tick in its place, so no answer is counted twice.
- Table: a clipboard cut-out. Each row is about two bubbles tall; its count box is on the right. Under the table is a sum line that stays empty until every bubble is sorted.
- Goal chip at the top of the stage: "Answers left: 8", counting down to 0. A second chip "Counts add up" appears when the activity is done.
3. Main Interaction
- Drag a bubble onto a row, or tap the bubble and then the row. The bubble shrinks and slides in, the count box grows by 1 with a small pop and "Answers left" goes down by 1.
- Tap a bubble that is already in a row to send it back; the count goes down by 1 (there is no Undo button). A bubble sits in one row only; a row holds any number of bubbles.
- Bottom buttons, three only: "Reset" (sends every bubble of this activity back), "Hint", "Next" (grey until the activity is done). No typing: every answer is a moved bubble or a tapped choice.
4. Activities
- Activity 1 (guided). Goal line: "Move every answer into its row." Goal chip: "Answers left: 8". Setup: the 8 bubbles above; rows "1 hour", "2 hours", "3 hours". Guess: before the first move, "Which row will get the most answers?" with three buttons, one per row. Result: counts 4, 2 and 2; the chip turns green with a gentle bounce; the row "1 hour" pulses; the sum line shows "4 + 2 + 2 = 8". Why line: "Four bubbles say 1 hr, so the row 1 hour has 4. 4 + 2 + 2 = 8 and we had 8 answers." Help: guided; the next bubble glows and the row names use the bubbles' words.
- Activity 2 (guided). Goal line: "Sort the answers, then check the counts." Goal chip: "Answers left: 9". Setup: 9 bubbles: 1 hr, 1/2 hr, 1 1/2 hr, 1 hr, 1/2 hr, 1 hr, 1 1/2 hr, 1 hr, 1 hr; rows "1/2 hour", "1 hour", "1 1/2 hour". Guess: "The counts of the three rows will add up to..." with buttons 8, 9, 10. Result: counts 2, 5 and 2; sum line "2 + 5 + 2 = 9". Why line: "2 + 5 + 2 = 9 and there are 9 answers, so every answer is in one row, once." After a guess of 8 or 10 it adds: "The counts always add up to the number of answers, 9." Help: guided; no bubble glows, the sum line is shown.
- Activity 3 (independent). Goal line: "A row can name a group. Sort every answer." Goal chip: "Answers left: 10". Setup: 10 bubbles: 1/2 hr, 1 1/2 hr, 1 hr, 2 hr, 1/2 hr, 1 1/2 hr, 1 hr, 1 1/2 hr, 1/2 hr, 2 hr; rows "1/2 hour", "1 hour", "More than 1 hour". Guess: "Which row will the 1 1/2 hr answers go in?" with the three row names as buttons. Result: counts 3, 2 and 5; sum line "3 + 2 + 5 = 10". Why line: "1 1/2 hr and 2 hr are both more than 1 hr, so they share one row. 3 + 2 + 5 = 10." Help: independent; only Hint.
- Star Challenge 1 (independent), the opener's own task. Goal line: "Sort all 35 answers into the table." Goal chip: "Answers left: 35". Setup: 35 faces in 5 rows of 7, bubbles in hours, in this order. Row 1: 1 1/2, 1, 1, 2 1/2, 1, 2 1/2, 1 1/2. Row 2: 1/2, 1/2, 1, 1, 1 1/2, 1 1/2, 2. Row 3: 2, 1/2, 1 1/2, 1, 1/2, 1/2, 1 1/2. Row 4: 1, 1, 1/2, 1, 2, 1/2, 1. Row 5: 1 1/2, 2 1/2, 1, 1/2, 1/2, 1, 1. Table rows: "1/2 hour", "1 hour", "1 1/2 hour", "2 hours", "More than 2 hours". Guess: "Which row will have the most children?" with the five row names as buttons. Result: counts 9, 13, 7, 3 and 3; the row "1 hour" pulses; sum line "9 + 13 + 7 + 3 + 3 = 35". Why line: "9 + 13 + 7 + 3 + 3 = 35. All 35 answers are in a row, once each." The three 2 1/2 hr bubbles go in "More than 2 hours", the three 2 hr bubbles in "2 hours". Help: independent.
5. Mathematical Understanding
- Moving every bubble turns a crowd into a table; each count is read from its count box.
- The child notices: each answer goes into exactly one row (the pale tick); the counts add up to the number of answers (the sum line); a row can name one answer ("2 hours") or a group ("More than 2 hours"); 2 1/2 hr is more than 2 hr; 2 hr is exactly 2 hours, not more.
- Rule: "Every answer goes in one row. The counts add up to the number of answers."
6. Feedback and Hints
- Correct: the bubble slides in, the count box pops, "Answers left" goes down. At the end the chip turns green with a gentle bounce and the sum line joins the counts with plus signs.
- Every wrong drop: the bubble bounces back, the strip turns red, the row shakes a little, ONE line says what to look at. Retry is free.
- Mistake: any wrong row -> the strip reads the bubble, for example "This bubble says 2 hr. Find the row with the same words." The bubble's words and the right row's words glow.
- Mistake: 1/2 hr put in "1 hour" -> "1/2 hr is half an hour, not 1 hour. Look for the row 1/2 hour." That row pulses.
- Mistake: 1 1/2 hr put in "1 hour" -> "This bubble says 1 1/2 hr, not 1 hr. Look at the number in front of the fraction." The whole number glows.
- Mistake: 2 1/2 hr put in "2 hours" -> "2 1/2 hr is more than 2 hr, so it goes in the row More than 2 hours." That row pulses.
- Mistake: 2 hr put in "More than 2 hours" -> "2 hr is exactly 2 hours, not more than 2 hours. Use the row 2 hours." The same for 1 hr in "More than 1 hour".
- Mistake: tapping a ticked place in the notebook -> "This answer is already in a row. Tap it in the row to take it out." The bubble in the row pulses.
- Mistake: Next pressed with bubbles left -> "2 answers are still in the notebook." The unticked bubbles pulse.
- Hints: (1) "Read the bubble. Which row has the same words?" (2) the next unsorted bubble glows and the border of its row glows (3) the bubble floats halfway to its row with an arrow and the child lets go.
- Edge cases: an answer exactly on a row's value (1 hr, 2 hr) stays in its own row; in every activity each row ends with at least 2 bubbles, so no count box stays at 0.
7. Ending
- Star Challenge 1 above. Success: all 35 bubbles are in rows, the counts are 9, 13, 7, 3 and 3, and the sum line shows 35.
- End screen: "Well done!" Remember: "Every answer goes in one row, once." "The counts of all the rows add up to the number of answers." "A row can name a group, like More than 2 hours." Think and talk: "Which row has the most children, and what does that tell you about the friends?" Button: "Start again". A small confetti burst plays here only.
8. Assets and Language
- Images: top-view photo of a wooden desk; spiral notebook page with blue lines (cut-out); clipboard with a table (cut-out, rows and count boxes drawn by code); 35 flat pen-and-ink faces in several skin tones and hair styles with speech-bubble outlines (bubble text drawn by code); small flat drawings of Samaira with a microphone and Kabir with a pen; a pale tick. English, hours written as 1/2 hr, 1 hr, 1 1/2 hr, 2 hr and 2 1/2 hr.

tool_config.idea: Turn a crowd of answers into a table: move every answer into the row where it belongs, read how many answers each row holds, check that the counts add up to the number of answers, and add rows to answer questions such as more than and less than. This is the free first try straight after the hook, so it asks and shows; the video that follows names the rule.
tool_config.title: Reporter's Notebook
tool_config.screen: The class newsroom desk of Samaira and Kabir, drawn as a warm, polished educational-game scene with soft shadows, cream and blue-grey wall tones and gentle animation. The notebook of your maths book lies open on the desk and is the largest thing on screen: 35 faces, and beside each face a speech bubble with its answer, 1/2 hr, 1 hr, 1 1/2 hr, 2 hr or 2 1/2 hr, in a mixed order. Next to the notebook stands the table with the headings No. of Hours Spent Watching TV and No. of Children and five rows, 1/2 hour, 1 hour, 1 1/2 hour, 2 hours and More than 2 hours, each row with a count box. On the practice cards a small practice notebook of 8 bubbles and a table with the three rows 1 hour, 2 hours and 3 hours take their place. On the first card one bubble glows to show where to start. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type, with progress dots under it. Controls: drag a bubble to a row, or tap the bubble and then tap the row, and the bubble slides into the row; tap a bubble that is already in a row to send it back to the notebook; a row bar for the more than and less than cards, where tapping a row adds its count to the bar (for example 2 + 2) and an answer box takes the number; answer boxes and a True and a False button for the four questions; Check, Hint, Undo (sends the last bubble back), Retry (returns the bubbles of this card to the notebook), Reset (empties the table), Back and Next in the same places on every card. Read-outs: a counter Answers still to sort (35 at the start, counting down to 0), the count box of each row, which grows by one at every drop, a pale tick in the notebook where a bubble has been sorted so that no answer is counted twice, and a sum line under the table that adds the counts of the rows (for example 4 + 2 + 2 = 8) and shows the number of answers beside it.
feedback: A bubble dropped in the right row slides in, the count box of that row grows by one, the counter Answers still to sort goes down by one, and a pale tick marks the bubble's place in the notebook so that no answer is counted twice.
A bubble dropped in the wrong row bounces back with a soft amber glow and a clue that reads the bubble aloud, for example: This answer says 2 hr, so it goes in the row 2 hours.
A bubble that says 2 1/2 hr dropped in the row 2 hours bounces back with: 2 1/2 hr is more than 2 hr, so it goes in the row More than 2 hours.

When every bubble is sorted, the sum line under the table adds the counts and says whether they add up, for example: 4 + 2 + 2 = 8. You had 8 answers, so every answer is in a row once. If a bubble is still in the notebook, the line says, for example: Your counts add up to 7. There are 8 answers, so one answer is not sorted yet.

On the more than and less than cards, a tapped row that does not belong gets a soft amber note, for example: The row 1 hour is not more than 1 hour. Tap the rows after it. A right set of rows shows their counts joined by plus signs, for example 2 + 2, and the answer box takes the sum.

In the four questions of your maths book a wrong answer gets a soft amber clue, never a red mark and never the answer, for example: Look again. Does the row 1/2 hour belong to more than half an hour? For the last question the clue says: Find the row 2 hours and the row 1/2 hour and compare the two counts.
tool_config.done_when: The 8 practice answers are sorted and read, the counts of the practice table add up to 8, the more than and less than cards are answered, the real notebook is sorted into the table with counts that add up to 35, and the four questions of your maths book are answered.

challenges: Card 1 (practice values): a small practice notebook has 8 answers, 2 hr, 1 hr, 3 hr, 1 hr, 2 hr, 1 hr, 3 hr and 1 hr. Move each bubble into its row of a table with the rows 1 hour, 2 hours and 3 hours. How many answers are in each row? Answer: the row 1 hour has 4, the row 2 hours has 2 and the row 3 hours has 2, and the counter Answers still to sort goes down to 0.

Card 2 (practice values): read the count box of each row and add the counts. Do they add up to the number of answers? Answer: yes, 4 + 2 + 2 = 8 and there are 8 answers, so every answer is in a row once. If the sum is not 8, an answer is missed or counted twice.

Card 3 (practice values): how many answered more than 1 hour? Tap the rows that are more than 1 hour and read the sum on the row bar. Answer: the rows 2 hours and 3 hours, 2 + 2 = 4. The row 1 hour is exactly 1 hour, not more, so it is not tapped.

Card 4 (practice values): how many answered less than 3 hours? Tap the rows that are less than 3 hours. Answer: the rows 1 hour and 2 hours, 4 + 2 = 6. The row 3 hours is exactly 3 hours, not less, so it is not tapped.

Challenge: 'Samaira and Kabir asked 35 friends: How many hours a day do you spend watching TV? Their answers are in the notebook. Fill in the number of children in each row of the table.' Sort all 35 answers of the real notebook into the five rows of the table and read the number of children in each row. Answer: 1/2 hour 9, 1 hour 13, 1 1/2 hour 7, 2 hours 3, More than 2 hours 3, and 9 + 13 + 7 + 3 + 3 = 35. The three 2 1/2 hr answers go in the row More than 2 hours.

Challenge: the book's four questions on the table, unchanged: 'Look at the table and answer the following questions.' First: 'How many children watch TV for more than half an hour?' Second: 'How many children watch TV for less than two hours?' Third: 'The number of children who watch TV for more than two hours is ___.' Fourth: 'More children watch TV for two hours than half an hour. (True/False)' Answers: first 26, because 13 + 7 + 3 + 3 = 26; second 29, because 9 + 13 + 7 = 29; third 3; fourth False, because 3 children watch for two hours and 9 children for half an hour, and 3 is less than 9. These questions are open: Check gives a clue and never shows the answer.

hint_ladder.text: Look at the answer in the bubble. Which row of the table has the same words as the bubble?

A row can name one answer, like 2 hours, or a group of answers, like More than 2 hours. Find the row where the bubble fits. For a question, ask which rows it asks about: the rows after a row for more than, the rows before a row for less than.

Match the words. A bubble that says 2 1/2 hr is more than 2 hours, so it belongs in the row More than 2 hours. For more than half an hour, the rows after the row 1/2 hour are 1 hour, 1 1/2 hour, 2 hours and More than 2 hours. Add their counts.

The tool slides the bubble into its row and says why, for example This answer says 2 hr, so it goes in the row 2 hours. For a question it lights up the rows to add and shows their counts joined by plus signs, then a similar card follows.

Move the 8 bubbles of a small practice notebook into the rows of a table, read the count of each row, check that the counts add up to the number of answers, and answer more than and less than questions by tapping rows and adding their counts.
Sort the 35 answers of the real notebook into the table of your maths book, then answer the book's four questions about the table, unchanged.

content.text:
1. Predict first: Kabir asks 12 friends how many hours a day they read. The answers are 1 hr, 2 hr, 1 hr, 1 hr, 3 hr, 2 hr, 1 hr, 2 hr, 1 hr, 3 hr, 1 hr and 2 hr. How can he show them so that anyone can read them quickly?
2. Make a table with one row for each kind of answer: 1 hour, 2 hours and 3 hours.
3. Move each answer into its row, once. Then count each row: the row 1 hour has 6 answers, the row 2 hours has 4 and the row 3 hours has 2.
4. Check that the counts add up to the number of friends: 6 + 4 + 2 = 12. If they do not, an answer was counted twice or missed.
5. A row can also name a group of answers, like the row More than 2 hours in your maths book's table. An answer of 2 1/2 hr goes in that row.
6. For more than 1 hour, add the rows after the row 1 hour: 4 + 2 = 6. The row 1 hour is not in it.
7. For less than 3 hours, add the rows before the row 3 hours: 6 + 4 = 10.
8. Can watching TV for a long time be harmful to the eyes? Think about it.
9. Rule: make one row for each kind of answer, count each row, and check that the counts add up to the number of friends.

content.text:
Worked example: Kabir asks 12 friends how many hours a day they read (practice values). The answers are 1 hr, 2 hr, 1 hr, 1 hr, 3 hr, 2 hr, 1 hr, 2 hr, 1 hr, 3 hr, 1 hr and 2 hr. Make a table and find how many friends read for more than 1 hour.
1. The answers are 1 hr, 2 hr or 3 hr, so the table has three rows: 1 hour, 2 hours and 3 hours.
2. Move the answers of 1 hr into the row 1 hour. They are the 1st, 3rd, 4th, 7th, 9th and 11th answers, so the row has 6 friends.
3. Move the answers of 2 hr into the row 2 hours. They are the 2nd, 6th, 8th and 12th answers, so the row has 4 friends.
4. Move the answers of 3 hr into the row 3 hours. They are the 5th and 10th answers, so the row has 2 friends.
5. More than 1 hour is the rows after the row 1 hour: the rows 2 hours and 3 hours. Add them: 4 + 2 = 6.
6. The 6 friends in the row 1 hour read for exactly 1 hour, not more, so they are left out.
7. Check: 6 + 4 + 2 = 12, so every answer was counted once. The 6 friends in the row 1 hour and the 6 friends who read for more than 1 hour add up to 6 + 6 = 12.
Answer: 6 friends read for more than 1 hour. The rows are 1 hour 6, 2 hours 4 and 3 hours 2, and 6 + 4 + 2 = 12.

5. $3$ bubbles say $2\text{ hr}$, so the row $2$ hours is $3$.
[Image: Child TV Reporter: Ans1: solution]
6. $3$ bubbles say $2 \frac{1}{2}\text{ hr}$. These answers are more than $2$ hours, so the three $2 \frac{1}{2}\text{ hr}$ answers go in the row More than $2$ hours: $3$.
7. Check: add the rows, $9 + 13 + 7 + 3 + 3 = 35$, the number of friends asked, so every answer is in a row once.
Answer: $\frac{1}{2}$ hour $9$, $1$ hour $13$, $1 \frac{1}{2}$ hour $7$, $2$ hours $3$, More than $2$ hours $3$, in all $35$ children.

media.title: Pictograph Maker
media.description:
A. TOOL TITLE
- Pictograph Maker
B. TOOL INFO
- Tool ID: M1.S4.T4.C17.2D1
- Tool type: Concept-activity
- Textbook source: Chapter 15 Data Through Pictures, Stock-Taking in a Shop: Dipesh's pictograph (1 icon = 5; Toys 8, Board games 10, Sports items 12 icons) and its four questions (developer only). Other numbers are practice values.
C. LEARNING OBJECTIVE
- The student sees that one icon can stand for many items, that the number of items is the number of icons times the scale, and that a scale must fit every number with nothing left over.
- Out of scope: comparing rows, bar graphs, scales above 10.
D. TOOL DESCRIPTION
1. Opening Screen
- Joseph Uncle's toy shop, as a photo: two wooden shelves on a cream wall. A green chalkboard above the lower shelf is the pictograph board: 3 rows, each with a name on the left and an empty lane for icons.
- A small icon box (a shop sign) at the top-left of the board reads "1 icon = 5 kites". Price tags on the shelf read "Kites 15", "Puzzles 25", "Balls 45". A wooden tray under the board holds a kite, a puzzle box and a ball icon.
- Instruction line: "Show each number with icons. One icon is 5." The kite icon glows; the child is invited to drag it into the Kites row.
2. Scene and Objects
- Board: about 70% of the stage width. A lane holds up to 15 icons on one line and up to 30 on two lines. Icons are about a thumb-width wide, photo-style cut-outs; every icon in a row is the same.
- Icon box: "1 icon = ___" with the scale number and item name, always visible.
- Scale chips: round wooden buttons 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10 above the board. In Activities 1 and 2 only 5 is active. A chip is greyed, with the note "Too many icons. Pick a bigger scale.", when a row would need more than 30 icons.
- Fit light: a lamp beside the icon box. Green when every number gives a whole number of icons; orange when some items are left over (a leftover tile shows beside the row).
- Row read-out, right of each lane, live: "3 icons of 5 each: 3 × 5 = 15". A chip at the top counts the rows done.
3. Main Interaction
- Drag an icon from the tray into its row, or tap the row's plus button. Tap an icon in a row to take it away (there is no Undo button).
- Tap a scale chip: the icon box changes and the board redraws at once. In Activities 3 and 4 the rows draw their icons by themselves; the child places icons only in Activity 1 and Star Challenge 3.
- Tap a row's "?" tag to flip it to its number (Activity 2). Typed answers use a big answer box with a number pad (0 to 9 and delete).
- Bottom buttons, three only: "Reset" (clears this activity), "Hint", "Check" (it turns into "Next" when the activity is done).
4. Activities
- Activity 1 (guided). Goal line: "Show each number with icons. One icon is 5." Goal chip: "Rows done: 0 of 3". Setup: scale 5; tags Kites 15, Puzzles 25, Balls 45; empty rows. Guess: before the first icon, "How many icons will the kites need?" with buttons 3, 5, 15. The child places 3, 5 and 9 icons. Result: each right row turns green with "3 icons of 5 each: 3 × 5 = 15", "5 icons of 5 each: 5 × 5 = 25", "9 icons of 5 each: 9 × 5 = 45". Why line: "15 ÷ 5 = 3, so the kites need 3 icons. One icon stands for 5 kites." Help: guided; read-outs are live.
- Activity 2 (guided). Goal line: "Read each row. How many items are there?" Goal chip: "Rows read: 0 of 3". Setup: scale 5; a ready board with Robots 11 icons, Drums 1 icon, Dolls 15 icons, each with a "?" tag. Guess: for each row the child picks a number from three buttons (Robots 11, 16 or 55; Drums 1, 5 or 6; Dolls 15, 20 or 75), then taps the "?" to flip the tag. Why lines: "11 icons of 5 each: 11 × 5 = 55 robots." "1 icon stands for 5 drums, so 1 × 5 = 5 drums." "15 icons of 5 each: 15 × 5 = 75 dolls." Help: guided.
- Activity 3 (independent). Goal line: "Try a bigger scale and a smaller scale." Goal chip: "Scales tried: 0 of 2". Setup: tags Cars 70, Bears 80, Dice 90; empty board; chips 3, 4, 5, 6, 10 (chip 2 is greyed: 35 icons or more). Guess: "Which scale needs fewer icons, 5 or 10?" with two buttons. The child taps chip 10 and chip 5 and the rows draw themselves. Result: scale 10 gives 7, 8 and 9 icons; scale 5 gives 14, 16 and 18. Why line: "Scale 10 needs 7 + 8 + 9 = 24 icons and scale 5 needs 14 + 16 + 18 = 48 icons. A bigger scale needs fewer icons." Help: independent.
- Activity 4 (independent). Goal line: "Find a scale that fits all three numbers." Goal chip: "Scale that fits". Setup: Cars 70, Bears 80, Dice 90. Guess: "Will a scale of 4 fit?" with Yes and No. The child taps chip 4 (lamp orange: "With 1 icon = 4, 70 items need 17 icons and 2 items are left over. Try another scale."), then other chips until the lamp is green (5 or 10). Why line for 10: "With 1 icon = 10: 70 ÷ 10 = 7, 80 ÷ 10 = 8 and 90 ÷ 10 = 9. Nothing is left over." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 1 (independent). Dipesh's pictograph is on the board: "1 train icon = 5 toys", "1 board game icon = 5 board games", "1 racket icon = 5 sports items"; rows Toys 8 train icons, Board games 10 board game icons, Sports items 12 racket icons. Goal chip: "Read the pictograph". The card asks, one after the other: "How many toys does Joseph Uncle have? ___" and "How many board games does Joseph Uncle have? ___" Guess: the typed number is the commitment; nothing shows until Check. Result: "Look at the icon box: 1 icon is 5 toys. 8 icons of 5 each: 8 × 5 = 40." and "10 icons of 5 each: 10 × 5 = 50." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 2 (independent). Goal chip: "Add the rows". The card asks: "How many total play items does Joseph Uncle have? ___" The child types the total. Result: the rows flip to 40, 50 and 60. Why line: "40 + 50 + 60 = 150. Check: 8 + 10 + 12 = 30 icons, and 30 icons of 5 each: 30 × 5 = 150." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 3 (independent, open). The card shows the book's sentence unchanged: "Is there any other scale that you can use to make the pictograph? Choose your scale and show the same data using a pictograph in your notebook." A small second line says "Build it on the empty board." Setup: empty board, tags Toys 40, Board games 50, Sports items 60, chips 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10. The child taps a chip (the commitment), sees the lamp, then drags icons into the rows. Result for scale 10: 4, 5 and 6 icons; why line "1 icon = 10. 40 ÷ 10 = 4, 50 ÷ 10 = 5 and 60 ÷ 10 = 6. Your answer may differ from this sample, and every scale that fits is right." For scale 2 the rows hold 20, 25 and 30 icons. Help: independent.
5. Mathematical Understanding
- One icon is a group of items. To read, count the icons and multiply by the scale; to draw, share the number into groups of the scale.
- Changing the scale shows that a bigger scale needs fewer icons, and that a number that does not share into groups leaves items over.
- Rules: "Number of items = number of icons × the scale." "A bigger scale needs fewer icons."
6. Feedback and Hints
- Correct: the row turns green with its number sentence; the goal chip bounces and turns green. Every wrong answer: red strip, a small shake, ONE friendly line, free retry.
- Mistake: one icon for every item (15 icons for 15 kites) -> "15 is the number of kites, not the number of icons. One icon stands for 5 kites." The icon box glows. A full row (30 icons) says "This row is full."
- Mistake: too many icons -> "You put 4 icons for 15 kites. 4 icons of 5 each: 4 × 5 = 20, but there are 15 kites." Too few -> "You put 2 icons for 15 kites. 2 icons of 5 each: 2 × 5 = 10, so 15 kites need more icons."
- Mistake: typing the number of icons (8 for the toys) -> "8 is the number of icons. One icon stands for 5 toys, so multiply the icons by 5." The toys row glows. Typing 30 for the total -> "30 is the number of icons. Each icon stands for 5 items. How many items do 30 icons stand for?"
- Mistake: guessing that scale 5 needs fewer icons than scale 10 -> "Look again. With a bigger scale each icon stands for more items, so fewer icons are needed."
- Mistake: Check on a scale that leaves items over -> "With 1 icon = 4, 70 items need 17 icons and 2 items are left over. Try another scale." (It names the first row that leaves items over.) Scale 5 in Star Challenge 3 -> "That is the scale Dipesh used. Choose a different scale."
- Hints: (1) "What does one icon stand for? Look at the icon box." (2) the icon box glows and the row's number shows brackets of 5 (3) the tool places all the icons but one, or fills in the icon count and leaves only the product.
- Edge cases: a row with one icon (Drums) still stands for 5 items; scale 1 is not offered (one icon for every item).
7. Ending
- Star Challenges 1 to 3 above. Success: both numbers and the total are right and a fitting scale other than 5 is shown with the right icons.
- End screen: "Well done!" Remember: "One icon stands for the scale." "Number of items = number of icons × the scale." "Choose a scale that fits every number, with nothing left over." Think and talk: "A shop has 500 toys. Which scale would you choose, and why?" Button: "Start again". A small confetti burst plays here only.
8. Assets and Language
- Images: toy-shop wall photo with wooden shelves; chalkboard (rows by code); wooden tray; price tags; photo cut-outs of a kite, puzzle box, ball, robot, drum, doll, toy car, teddy bear, dice set, toy train, board game box and racket; wooden scale chips; a lamp. English.

tool_config.idea: Show numbers with icons using a scale: choose the scale, place the icons of each row, read a row back as the number of icons × the scale, and see that a bigger scale needs fewer icons and that the scale must fit every number with nothing left over.
tool_config.title: Pictograph Maker
tool_config.screen: Joseph Uncle's shop shelf in the class newsroom, drawn as a warm, polished educational-game scene with soft shadows, cream and blue-grey wall tones and gentle animation. On the left a small table of items with their numbers, with the headings Name of the Item and Number of Items. On the right the pictograph strip is the largest thing on screen: three rows, each with its name and room for icons, and an icon box at the top of the strip that reads 1 icon = ___ items and changes with the scale. Above the strip is the scale box 1 icon = ___ with a stepper that picks any whole number from 1 to 12 and quick buttons 1, 2, 5 and 10. Below the strip is a tray of icons in the pictures of your maths book: a train for toys, a board game, a racket for sports items and a scooter for two-wheelers. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type, with progress dots under it. On the reading cards the strip comes ready with its icons and a number box appears beside each row. Controls: pick the scale with the stepper or a quick button; drag an icon from the tray into a row, or tap a row to add one icon; tap an icon in a row to take it away; a Show the number switch that turns the icons of a row into its number; number boxes for typing an answer; Check, Hint, Undo, Retry (clears the icons of this card), Reset (clears the strip and the scale), Back and Next in the same places on every card. Read-outs: for each row a line icons × scale = number (for example 3 × 5 = 15), the total number of icons, and a fit light beside the scale box that is green when every number gives a whole number of icons and soft amber when some items would be left over, with a note that says how many. When some items are left over, the tool places no icon for them and asks for another scale.
feedback: A right row shows its read-out in soft green, for example 3 icons, 3 × 5 = 15. This row is right.

Too many icons gets a soft amber note, for example: You put 7 icons for 30 items. One icon is 5 items, so 30 items need 6 icons. Too few icons gets, for example: You put 5 icons for 30 items. 5 × 5 = 25, so 30 items need more icons.
A scale that does not fit turns the fit light amber with, for example: With one icon = 4, 30 items need 7 icons and 2 items are left over. Try another scale.
A wrong number when reading a row back gets a clue about the scale, for example: You wrote 9 for the toys. 9 is the number of icons. One icon stands for 5 toys, so multiply the icons by the scale.

When the scale changes, the strip redraws at once and the tool says how many icons each row needs now, for example: With 1 icon = 10, 20 items need 2 icons. With 1 icon = 5, they need 4 icons. A bigger scale needs fewer icons.

The choose-your-scale items are never marked wrong when the scale fits. The tool checks that every number gives a whole number of icons, shows the read-out of each row and says: Your answer may differ from the sample, and every scale that fits is right.
tool_config.done_when: A practice stock is shown with the scale 5, a ready pictograph is read back, the scales 10, 5 and 4 are tried on the same numbers, Dipesh's three questions are answered, and a scale that fits is chosen for Dipesh's data and for Deepti's data.

challenges: Card 1 (practice values): set 1 icon = 5 and show a practice stock of toys 15, board games 30 and sports items 25. How many icons does each row need? Answer: 3 icons for the toys, because 15 ÷ 5 = 3; 6 icons for the board games, because 30 ÷ 5 = 6; 5 icons for the sports items, because 25 ÷ 5 = 5.

Card 2 (practice values): a ready pictograph has 1 icon = 5 items, with toys 9 icons, board games 11 icons and sports items 6 icons. Press Show the number for each row. How many items are in each row? Answer: 9 × 5 = 45 toys, 11 × 5 = 55 board games and 6 × 5 = 30 sports items.

Card 3 (practice values): the numbers are 20, 30 and 50 items. Set the scale to 10 and place the icons. How many icons does each row need? Answer: 2, 3 and 5 icons, because 20 ÷ 10 = 2, 30 ÷ 10 = 3 and 50 ÷ 10 = 5.

Card 4 (practice values): change the scale of the same numbers, 20, 30 and 50, to 5. How many icons does each row need now, and which scale needs fewer icons? Answer: 4, 6 and 10 icons, because 20 ÷ 5 = 4, 30 ÷ 5 = 6 and 50 ÷ 5 = 10. The bigger scale 10 needs fewer icons.

Card 5 (practice values): change the scale of the same numbers to 4. Does it fit? Answer: no. 20 ÷ 4 = 5 fits, but 30 ÷ 4 is 7 with 2 left over and 50 ÷ 4 is 12 with 2 left over, so the fit light turns amber and the tool asks for another scale.

media.teaching_notes: Predict first: a shop has 35 erasers. Drawing one picture for each eraser is too much work. What could the shopkeeper do? Use one icon for 5 erasers. This is what Dipesh suggests to Joseph Uncle: one icon for every 5 items. The icon box tells what one icon stands for. It is called the scale: 1 icon = 5 items. 7 icons show 35 erasers, because 7 × 5 = 35. That is 7 icons instead of 35 pictures. To read a pictograph, count the icons in a row and multiply by the scale. Rule: the number of items = the number of icons × the scale. A scale helps record a large number of things using fewer icons. 1. The scale is 1 icon = 5 items, so each row needs as many icons as there are groups of 5 in its number. 2. Pens: 10 ÷ 5 = 2, so the row has 2 icons. 3. Pencils: 20 ÷ 5 = 4, so the row has 4 icons. 4. Erasers: 35 ÷ 5 = 7, so the row has 7 icons. 5. Read the rows back, icons × scale: 2 × 5 = 10 pens, 4 × 5 = 20 pencils and 7 × 5 = 35 erasers. 6. Count all the icons: 2 + 4 + 7 = 13 icons, and 13 × 5 = 65 items in all. 7. Check: 10 + 20 + 35 = 65, the same 65 items. Answer: Pens 2 icons, pencils 4 icons and erasers 7 icons. The 13 icons stand for 65 items.

topics.summary: A scale lets one icon stand for several items, so a large number needs fewer icons. The number of items is the number of icons × the scale, and a scale must fit every number with nothing left over.

content.text:
Joseph Uncle takes stock of the play items (toys, board games, and sports items) in his store a week before the summer break. He tries to record the items in his shop using a pictograph.
He notices that there are too many items of each kind in his shop and it is not easy to make a picture for every item.
How can I show these with pictures?
Suggest some ways to him.
Dipesh, one of his helpers, suggested using one picture (icon) for every 5 items of each kind.
Dipesh used a scale while recording the items in the pictograph. A scale helps record a large number of things using fewer icons.

content.text:
1. Predict first: a shop has 35 erasers. Drawing one picture for each eraser is too much work. What could the shopkeeper do?
2. Use one icon for 5 erasers. This is what Dipesh suggests to Joseph Uncle: one icon for every 5 items.
3. The icon box tells what one icon stands for. It is called the scale: 1 icon = 5 items.
4. 7 icons show 35 erasers, because 7 × 5 = 35. That is 7 icons instead of 35 pictures.
5. To read a pictograph, count the icons in a row and multiply by the scale.
6. Rule: the number of items = the number of icons × the scale. A scale helps record a large number of things using fewer icons.

content.text:
Worked example: A stationery shop has 10 pens, 20 pencils and 35 erasers (practice values). Show them in a pictograph where one icon stands for 5 items, then read the pictograph back.
{{DIAGRAM:M1.S4.T4.C15.IMG2}}
1. The scale is 1 icon = 5 items, so each row needs as many icons as there are groups of 5 in its number.
2. Pens: 10 ÷ 5 = 2, so the row has 2 icons.
3. Pencils: 20 ÷ 5 = 4, so the row has 4 icons.
4. Erasers: 35 ÷ 5 = 7, so the row has 7 icons.
5. Read the rows back, icons × scale: 2 × 5 = 10 pens, 4 × 5 = 20 pencils and 7 × 5 = 35 erasers.
6. Count all the icons: 2 + 4 + 7 = 13 icons, and 13 × 5 = 65 items in all.
7. Check: 10 + 20 + 35 = 65, the same 65 items.
Answer: Pens 2 icons, pencils 4 icons and erasers 7 icons. The 13 icons stand for 65 items.

One icon stands for the scale, so the number of items = the number of icons × the scale.
To find a total, find every row and add them, or add all the icons and multiply by the scale.
A scale must fit every number, with nothing left over.
The same data can be shown with another scale that fits.

Try a scale of 10: 40 ÷ 10 = 4, 50 ÷ 10 = 5 and 60 ÷ 10 = 6. Every number fits.
With 1 icon standing for 10 items, toys have 4 icons, board games have 5 icons and sports items have 6 icons.
A scale of 2 fits too, with 20, 25 and 30 icons. A scale of 4 does not fit, because 50 ÷ 4 is 12 with 2 left over.
Draw the icons of each row and write the icon box: 1 icon stands for 10 items.
Check: read back, 4 × 10 = 40, 5 × 10 = 50 and 6 × 10 = 60, the same numbers as before.

How many more? Find the difference: 70 − 30 = 40. You can also take the icons first: 7 − 3 = 4 icons, and 4 × 10 = 40. For the total of the two days, add the rows: 30 + 70 = 100. 1. Predict first: a snack stall's pictograph has 3 icons for Tuesday and 7 icons for Thursday, and one icon = 10 samosas. Which day sold more samosas, and how many more?
2. Read each row, icons × scale. Tuesday: 3 × 10 = 30 samosas. Thursday: 7 × 10 = 70 samosas.
3. When every icon stands for the same number, the row with more icons is more. So Thursday sold more.
4. How many more? Find the difference: 70 − 30 = 40. You can also take the icons first: 7 − 3 = 4 icons, and 4 × 10 = 40.
5. For the total of the two days, add the rows: 30 + 70 = 100. You can also add the icons first: 3 + 7 = 10 icons, and 10 × 10 = 100.
6. Rule: read each row as icons × scale. The most is the biggest number, the total is all the rows added, and how many more or fewer is the difference.

content.text:
Worked example: A snack stall's pictograph (practice values): one icon = 10 samosas. Tuesday has 3 icons, Thursday has 7 icons and Saturday has 2 icons. Which day sold the most, how many samosas were sold in all, how many fewer on Saturday than on Tuesday and how many more on Thursday than on Saturday?
{{DIAGRAM:M1.S6.T6.C26.IMG2}}
1. Read each row, icons × scale: Tuesday 3 × 10 = 30, Thursday 7 × 10 = 70 and Saturday 2 × 10 = 20 samosas.
2. The most: 70 is more than 30 and 20, so Thursday sold the most, 70 samosas.
3. Count all the icons: 3 + 7 + 2 = 12 icons, and 12 × 10 = 120 samosas in all.
4. Fewer on Saturday than on Tuesday: find the difference, 30 − 20 = 10.
5. More on Thursday than on Saturday: find the difference, 70 − 20 = 50.
6. Check: add the three rows, 30 + 70 + 20 = 120, the same 120 samosas.
Answer: Thursday sold the most, 70. In all 120 samosas. Saturday sold 10 fewer than Tuesday, and Thursday sold 50 more than Saturday.

content.text:
1. Icon box: $1$ scooter icon stands for $3$ two-wheelers. Count the icons: Monday $8$, Wednesday $4$, Friday $12$.
2. Monday: $8 \times 3 = 24$ two-wheelers.
3. Wednesday: $4 \times 3 = 12$ two-wheelers.
4. Friday: $12 \times 3 = 36$ two-wheelers.
5. Compare: $36$ is more than $24$ and $12$, so Friday has the most.
[Image: Two-wheelers on the Road: Ans1: solution]
6. Check: Friday has the most icons too, $12$ icons, and every icon stands for $3$.
Answer: Friday, with $36$ two-wheelers.

media.title: Squares to Bars
media.description:
A. TOOL TITLE
- Squares to Bars
B. TOOL INFO
- Tool ID: M2.S8.T8.C40.2D1
- Tool type: Concept-activity
- Textbook source: Chapter 15 Data Through Pictures, Recording a Day: Raman's table (one square = 1 hour: sleeping 9, school 6, studying 2, eating and playing 6, other activities 1), Sheela's bar graph (8, 7, 4, 3, 2) and the book's five questions (developer only). Samaira's and Kabir's weeks are practice values.
C. LEARNING OBJECTIVE
- The student sees that a row of squares stands up into a bar of the same height, reads the height of a bar on the vertical line, and compares two bars to say which is more and by how many.
- Out of scope: making a graph from a table of numbers, scales other than 1 square = 1 hour, totals of all bars.
D. TOOL DESCRIPTION
1. Opening Screen
- A classroom wall as a photo. On the left a cork pinboard holds three rows of glossy blue square tiles, each tile about a thumb-width: Homework 4, Games 2, TV 1. Each row has its name at the left end and its count under it ("4 squares").
- On the right an empty graph board in a wooden frame: the vertical line marked 0 to 10 and named "Number of Hours", the horizontal base named "Activities" with three places, and a thin dotted guide from each row to its place.
- Instruction line: "Stand each row up. The bar is as tall as the row is long."
- The Homework row glows. The child is invited to tap a mark on the vertical line first, then the row.
2. Scene and Objects
- Tiles are drawn by code, 1 square = 1 hour. The graph board is grid paper with equal marks and numbers 0 to 10. Bars are solid, all the same width, one colour per graph (warm orange; a second graph is sky blue). No number is printed on a bar.
- Reading line: a thin horizontal rod with a round handle, resting at 0, with a small tag showing the number it points to. Guess flag: a small flag the child drops on a mark. Goal chip at the top, for example "Bars: 0 of 3".
- Activity 4 shows two graphs side by side with the same marks. In the challenges the stage holds Raman's table on the left, Raman's empty graph in the middle and Sheela's graph on the right; once all five rows are up the table folds into a tab so the two graphs share the stage.
3. Main Interaction
- Tap a row of squares: it stands up with a soft slide into a bar of the same height; its row stays as a pale ghost. Tap the small "lay down" arrow on a bar to lay it back (there is no Undo button).
- Drag the reading line up or down; it snaps to whole marks. Tap two bars to compare them (a third tap replaces the older one).
- Activity 3 only: a small plus and minus at the foot of the TV bar add or take away one square.
- Bottom buttons, three only: "Reset", "Hint", "Check" (it turns into "Next" when the activity is done). Typed answers use a number pad.
4. Activities
- Activity 1 (guided). Goal line: "Stand each row up. The bar is as tall as the row is long." Goal chip: "Bars: 0 of 3". Setup: Samaira's week, Homework 4, Games 2, TV 1 squares (practice values). Guess: before touching the Homework row, the child drops a flag on the mark where the top of its bar will reach. Result: each tapped row stands up; the flag turns green if it was at 4, otherwise the strip adds "Your flag was at 6. The bar reaches 4." (with the child's own number). Why line: "The homework row has 4 squares, so the bar goes up to 4." Help: guided; counts and dotted guides are shown.
- Activity 2 (guided). Goal line: "Slide the line to the top of each bar and read the number." Goal chip: "Bars read: 0 of 3". Setup: the three bars stand; the line is at 0. Guess: "Which bar is the tallest?" The child taps a bar. Result: with the line on each top the tag reads 4, 2 and 1 and each bar gets a tick. Why line: "The line touches the top of the homework bar at 4, so it is 4 hours high. Homework is the tallest and TV is the shortest." Help: guided; the line snaps gently near a top.
- Activity 3 (independent). Goal line: "Make the TV bar as tall as the homework bar." Goal chip: "TV = Homework". Setup: TV bar 1 high, homework bar 4 high. Guess: "How many squares must be added?" with buttons 2, 3, 4. The child taps plus. Result: the TV bar rises to 4 and the chip turns green. Why line: "The TV bar was 1 high and the homework bar is 4 high. 4 − 1 = 3, so 3 squares were added." Help: independent.
- Activity 4 (guided, then independent). Goal line: "Tap two bars of the same activity. Who spent more time?" Goal chip: "Compared: 0 of 3". Setup: Samaira's graph (orange: Homework 4, Games 2, TV 1) beside Kabir's graph (blue: Homework 3, Games 4, TV 1), practice values. Guess, before each pair: the child taps "Samaira", "Kabir" or "The same". Result: a dotted line joins the two tops. Why lines: "Samaira's bar is 4 high and Kabir's is 3 high. 4 − 3 = 1, so Samaira spent 1 hour more." "Kabir's bar is 4 high and Samaira's is 2 high. 4 − 2 = 2, so Kabir spent 2 hours more." "Both bars are 1 high, so the time is the same." Help: guided for homework (the dotted line shows after the first tap); independent for games and TV.
- Star Challenge 1 (independent). Raman's five rows lie on the pinboard (Time spent sleeping 9, Time in school 6, Time spent studying 2, Time spent eating and playing 6, Other activities 1 squares). The child stands each up in Raman's graph beside Sheela's bar graph (Sleeping 8, Time in school 7, Studying 4, Eating and playing 3, Other activities 2). Goal chip: "Stand up Raman's 5 rows". Then three questions, one at a time, in the book's words: "Whose daily routine shows more time spent on sleeping? ___" (tap "Raman" or "Sheela"), "Who spends more hours in the school? ___" (tap a name), "How many more hours does Sheela spend studying compared to Raman? ___" (number pad). Guess: the child's own answer is the commitment. Results: "Raman's sleeping bar is 9 high and Sheela's is 8 high. 9 is more than 8, so Raman." "Raman's school bar is 6 high and Sheela's is 7 high, so Sheela." "Sheela's studying bar is 4 high and Raman's is 2 high. 4 − 2 = 2 hours more."
- Star Challenge 2 (independent). The same two graphs. Question 4, in the book's words: "Is there any activity on which they spend the same amount of time? If yes, name the activity ___" The child taps "No" or one of the five activity names. Result: each pair of bars lights in turn: "9 and 8, 6 and 7, 2 and 4, 6 and 3, 1 and 2. All five pairs are different, so the answer is No." Question 5: "Based on their data, whose routine do you think is more balanced? Why? ___" The child taps "Raman" or "Sheela", then taps two bars of that child as the reason; the tool says how far apart the two bars are. Sample shown after Check: "Sample answer: Sheela's, because her studying 4 and eating and playing 3 are closer than Raman's 2 and 6. Your answer may differ." Help: independent.
5. Mathematical Understanding
- Standing a row up shows that squares and bar are the same data: the bar is as tall as the row is long. The number is read where the top meets the vertical line, never from the width.
- Comparing shows the taller bar is more, equal tops are the same, and the gap between two tops is how many more.
- Rules: "A bar is as tall as its row of squares is long." "The taller bar is more. Take the smaller from the bigger to find how many more."
6. Feedback and Hints
- Correct: a green tick, a gentle bounce, one line with the numbers. Every wrong answer: red strip, a small shake, ONE friendly line, free retry.
- Mistake: line not on the top -> "The line is above the bar. Slide it down until it touches the top." or "The bar is taller. Slide the line up until it touches the top." The top pulses.
- Mistake: wrong number of squares in Activity 3 -> "The TV bar is now 5 high but the homework bar is 4 high. Take one square away." or "The TV bar is 3 high. One more square makes it 4."
- Mistake: the shorter bar named as more -> "Look again. The taller bar is the one with more hours. Which of the two bars is taller?" Both tops pulse.
- Mistake: adding instead of taking away -> "4 + 2 = 6 adds the two heights. To find how many more, take the smaller height from the bigger." Answering 4 for the studying question -> "4 is Sheela's hours. How many more is that than Raman's 2?"
- Mistake: "Time in school" or "Eating and playing" for question 4 (Raman has 6 and 6) -> "Raman has 6 hours for school and 6 for eating and playing, but those are two activities of one child. Compare the same activity of Raman and Sheela." The five pairs light up.
- Mistake: width used as the number -> "All the bars have the same width. Only the height tells the number of hours."
- Hints: (1) "How many squares are in this row? The bar is that tall." (2) dotted lines run from the tops to the vertical line (3) the reading line moves to the top of the bar, or both heights are shown and only the answer is left.
- Edge cases: two tops at the same height show "the same", never "0 more"; the open question never turns red and accepts any reason with two bars.
7. Ending
- Star Challenges 1 and 2 above. Success: all five rows stand up and all five questions are answered; question 5 needs a name and two bars.
- End screen: "Well done!" Remember: "A bar is as tall as its row of squares is long." "Read a bar where its top meets the vertical line." "The taller bar is more. Take the smaller from the bigger to find how many more." Think and talk: "Why do all the bars have the same width?" Button: "Start again". A small confetti burst plays here only.
8. Assets and Language
- Images: classroom wall photo with a cork pinboard; glossy blue square tile; wooden-framed graph board with grid paper; reading rod; small flag; arrow icon. Bars and marks by code. English.

tool_config.idea: See that a row of squares stands up into a bar of the same height, read the height of a bar on the vertical line with a sliding reading line, and compare two children's bars. The squares and the bars are the same data in two forms, and this tool is where the student sees one turn into the other.
tool_config.title: Squares to Bars
tool_config.screen: The graph wall of Samaira and Kabir's class newsroom, drawn as a warm, polished educational-game scene with soft shadows and gentle animation, in soft cream and blue-grey wall tones. The table and the graph are the largest things on screen and nothing else competes with them. On the left, pinned to the wall, is a table with one row for each activity: each row is a line of blue squares, one square stands for 1 hour, and the name of the activity sits at the left end of the row. On the right is an empty graph on a grid: the vertical line is marked 0 to 10 in equal steps and called Number of Hours, and the horizontal base has one place for each activity and is called Activities. A thin dotted guide joins each row to its place on the base. A reading line, a thin horizontal bar with a small round handle, rests at 0 and slides up and down the vertical line, and a small tag on it shows the number it points to. A Compare switch under the graph puts a second graph beside the first, with the same marks, so that two children's bars stand side by side. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type, with progress dots under it. Controls: tap a row of squares and it stands up into a solid bar of the same height on its place on the base, with a soft slide and settle; a small Lay down arrow on a standing bar lays it down again into its row; a small plus and a small minus at the end of a row add or take away one square (on the practice cards only); drag the reading line up or down and let go on the top of a bar; tap two bars to compare them; on the first card only, tap a mark on the vertical line to place a guess marker before a row is stood up; the Compare switch; Check; Hint; Undo, which lays down the row that was stood up last; Retry, which lays the squares of this step down again; Reset, which lays all the rows down; Back and Next in the same places on every card. Read-outs: the number of squares counted under each row (for example 4 squares), the number on the tag of the reading line, the heights of the two bars chosen with a word beside them (more, the same, or how many more, for example 4 − 3 = 1), and a card number out of 7. In the cards of your maths book the table holds Raman's five rows, as in your maths book, and the compare graph holds Sheela's five bars. Every bar has the same width and each graph has one friendly colour, in the warm colour of Sheela's bars for the first graph and soft sky blue for the second. The bar or number being asked about glows bright tangerine, a right answer turns green, and a look again note is soft amber, never red.
feedback: When a row is tapped it stands up and the tool says what happened, for example: The row has 4 squares, so the bar goes up to 4.

If the reading line is not yet on the top of a bar, the tag shows a soft amber note: The bar is taller. Slide the line up until it touches the top. Or: The line is above the bar. Slide it down until it touches the top.
A wrong reading shows a soft amber note: Look again. Read the height where the top of the bar meets the vertical line. The line is at 4 here, so the bar is 4 high.
When two bars are tapped the tool says how they compare, for example: Samaira's bar is 4 high and Kabir's is 3 high. 4 is more than 3, and 4 − 3 = 1, so Samaira spent 1 hour more.
When two bars are the same height the tool says: Both bars are 1 high, so the time is the same.
If the student picks the shorter bar as the one with more time, a soft amber note says: Look again. The taller bar is the one with more hours. Which of the two bars is taller?
All bars have the same width, and the tool says so when a bar is chosen: Only the height tells the number of hours, so a wider bar would not be a bigger number.

For the open question about a more balanced routine the tool accepts any answer whose reason names two numbers from the graph, and says: Good. Your reason uses the numbers. Another answer can be right too.
tool_config.done_when: The student has stood up all three rows of Samaira's week, read each height with the reading line, made a bar as tall as another bar, compared Samaira's and Kabir's practice graphs, and then answered the five questions on Raman's and Sheela's days using the compare view.

challenges: Card 1 (practice values): Samaira's week has homework 4 squares, games 2 squares and TV 1 square. Tap each row to stand it up. How tall is each bar? Answer: the homework bar is 4 high, the games bar is 2 high and the TV bar is 1 high. Each bar is as tall as its row is long.

Card 2: drag the reading line to the top of each bar and read the number on the vertical line. Which bar is the tallest and which is the shortest? Answer: the reading line says 4 at the homework bar, 2 at the games bar and 1 at the TV bar. Homework is the tallest and TV is the shortest.

Card 3: make a bar as tall as another bar. Add squares to the TV row until its bar is as tall as the games bar. How many squares did you add? Answer: 1 square. The TV row has 1 square, the games bar is 2 high, and 2 − 1 = 1.

Card 5: tap the two games bars, then the two TV bars. Who spent more time on games, and by how many hours? Is there an activity with the same time? Answer: Kabir spent more time on games, by 4 − 2 = 2 hours. TV is the same: both bars are 1 high, so each child watched for 1 hour.

Answers: No, the hours are different on all five activities (9 and 8, 6 and 7, 2 and 4, 6 and 3, 1 and 2). media.teaching_notes: Predict first: Kabir's reading row has 3 squares and Samaira's reading bar is 4 high. Who read for longer, and by how many hours? To read a bar, find its top and look straight across to the vertical line. The number there is the height. Read the height where the top meets the vertical line. A taller bar is more. Two bars of the same height show the same amount. To find how many more, take the smaller height from the bigger height. Samaira's 4 and Kabir's 3 give 4 − 3 = 1, so Samaira read for 1 hour more. Compare the two children activity by activity, and say for each one who has more, how many more, or that the two are the same. Rule: read each bar by its height on the vertical line, the taller bar is more, and the difference of the two heights is how many more. 1. Read Kabir's rows by counting the squares: reading 3, playing 5 and helping at home 2. 2. Read Samaira's bars where each top meets the vertical line: reading 4, playing 3 and helping at home 2. 3. Reading: Samaira 4 hours and Kabir 3 hours. 4 is more than 3, so Samaira read for longer. 4. How many hours more? 4 − 3 = 1 hour more. 5. Playing: Kabir 5 hours and Samaira 3 hours. Kabir played more, by 5 − 3 = 2 hours. 6. Helping at home: Kabir 2 hours and Samaira 2 hours. The two bars are the same height, so the time is the same. 7. Check: the heights differ for reading, by 1, and for playing, by 2, and are equal only for helping at home. Answer: Samaira read 1 hour more. Kabir played 2 hours more. Helping at home is the same, 2 hours

{{DIAGRAM:M2.S8.T8.C38.IMG2}}
1. Write the three activities along the horizontal base: reading, playing and helping at home.
2. Mark the vertical line 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 for the number of hours. The tallest row has 5 squares, so the line goes past 5.
3. Stand the reading row up. It has 3 squares, so the reading bar is 3 high.
4. Stand the playing row up. It has 5 squares, so the playing bar is 5 high.
5. Stand the helping at home row up. It has 2 squares, so that bar is 2 high.
6. Check: each bar is as tall as its row is long, 3, 5 and 2. Add the heights: 3 + 5 + 2 = 10 hours in all.
Answer: Bars of height 3, 5 and 2. Kabir spent 3 + 5 + 2 = 10 hours on these three activities

content.text:
1. Predict first: Kabir's reading row has 3 squares and Samaira's reading bar is 4 high. Who read for longer, and by how many hours?
2. To read a bar, find its top and look straight across to the vertical line. The number there is the height. Read the height where the top meets the vertical line.
3. A taller bar is more. Two bars of the same height show the same amount.
4. To find how many more, take the smaller height from the bigger height. Samaira's 4 and Kabir's 3 give 4 − 3 = 1, so Samaira read for 1 hour more.
5. Compare the two children activity by activity, and say for each one who has more, how many more, or that the two are the same.
6. Rule: read each bar by its height on the vertical line, the taller bar is more, and the difference of the two heights is how many more.

content.text:
Worked example: Kabir's Saturday has rows of squares: reading 3, playing 5 and helping at home 2. Samaira's bar graph of her Saturday has bars: reading 4, playing 3 and helping at home 2 (practice values). Who spent more time reading, and by how many hours? Who played more, and by how many hours? On which activity did they spend the same time?
{{DIAGRAM:M2.S8.T8.C39.IMG2}}
1. Read Kabir's rows by counting the squares: reading 3, playing 5 and helping at home 2.
2. Read Samaira's bars where each top meets the vertical line: reading 4, playing 3 and helping at home 2.
3. Reading: Samaira 4 hours and Kabir 3 hours. 4 is more than 3, so Samaira read for longer.
4. How many hours more? 4 − 3 = 1 hour more.
5. Playing: Kabir 5 hours and Samaira 3 hours. Kabir played more, by 5 − 3 = 2 hours.
6. Helping at home: Kabir 2 hours and Samaira 2 hours. The two bars are the same height, so the time is the same.
7. Check: the heights differ for reading, by 1, and for playing, by 2, and are equal only for helping at home.
Answer: Samaira read 1 hour more. Kabir played 2 hours more. Helping at home is the same, 2 hours

content.text:
1. A balanced day gives fair time to each activity, so the hours are not very far apart. Look at studying and at eating and playing.
2. Raman studies $2$ hours and plays $6$ hours. The two are far apart: $6 - 2 = 4$ hours.
3. Sheela studies $4$ hours and plays $3$ hours. The two are close: $4 - 3 = 1$ hour.
[Image: Recording a Day: Ans5: solution]
4. Sheela's studying and playing are closer together, so her routine is more balanced.

media.title: Bar Graph Builder
media.description:
A. TOOL TITLE
- Bar Graph Builder
B. TOOL INFO
- Tool ID: M2.S10.T10.C53.2D1
- Tool type: Concept-activity
- Textbook source: Chapter 15 Data Through Pictures, Day in My Life (record the 24 hours, make a bar graph) and Whose Index Finger is Longer? (five paper strips, four questions); the book's sheets have the vertical line marked 0 to 9 and 1 to 10 with 1 cm at the foot (developer only). All sample numbers are practice values.
C. LEARNING OBJECTIVE
- The student sees how to make a bar graph: names along the horizontal base, a vertical line that reaches at least the biggest number, and each bar drawn up to its number or its length in cm.
- Out of scope: comparing two graphs, minutes, scales other than 1 hour or 1 cm per mark.
D. TOOL DESCRIPTION
1. Opening Screen
- A wooden drawing board with a sheet of graph paper (photo texture), a pencil and a ruler beside it. The vertical line is marked 0 to 10 and named "Number of Hours"; the horizontal base is named "Activities" with three empty name places, each with a small round knob at its foot.
- A small paper table pinned at the top-left: "School 5", "Studying 3", "Sleeping 7". Three paper name tags, "School", "Studying", "Sleeping", lie in a tray under the sheet.
- Instruction line: "Write the names on the base. Make each bar as tall as its number."
- The tag "School" glows. The child is invited to drag it onto the first place.
2. Scene and Objects
- Sheet: about 70% of the stage. Marks are equal; every bar and strip has the same width. Bars are warm orange; the bar being asked about glows tangerine. A small tag at a bar's top shows its height.
- Name tags are paper cut-outs. In the length activities the tray holds coloured paper strips and the vertical line is a ruler: 1 cm at the foot, then 2, 3 and so on to 10.
- Goal chip at the top, for example "Bars: 0 of 3"; a "Total" chip adds the table's numbers.
3. Main Interaction
- Drag a name tag onto a place on the base. Drag the round knob of a place up or down: the bar grows to the nearest whole mark. Tap a name on the base to take it back (there is no Undo button).
- Activity 2 only: an up arrow at the top of the vertical line adds one mark (to at most 12).
- Day in My Life: each table row has a minus and a plus around its hours; "Hours left" counts from 24. A chip "Use sample day" fills 9, 5, 2, 2, 3, 3 (whole hours only).
- Finger strips: five strips (Mine, Friend 1 to Friend 4); drag a strip's top to the length you measured outside the tool, 1 to 10 cm. A chip "Use sample strips" fills 6, 7, 5, 8, 6.
- Bottom buttons, three only: "Reset", "Hint", "Check" (it turns into "Next" when done). Typed answers use a number pad.
4. Activities
- Activity 1 (guided). Goal line: "Write the names on the base. Make each bar as tall as its number." Goal chip: "Bars: 0 of 3". Setup: table School 5, Studying 3, Sleeping 7 (practice values), line 0 to 10. Guess: before building, "Which bar will be the tallest?" with the three names as buttons. Result: bars at 5, 3 and 7; the tallest glows. Why line: "Sleeping is 7 hours, so the bar goes up to 7. 5 + 3 + 7 = 15 hours." Help: guided; each name tag matches the table and the target marks glow faintly.
- Activity 2 (guided). Goal line: "Make the line tall enough, then draw the bars." Goal chip: "Line and bars". Setup: Sunday table Playing 6, TV 3, Reading 2 (practice values); names already on the base; the line is marked 0 to 4 only. Guess: "How far must the line go?" with buttons "Up to 4", "Up to 6", "Up to 10". Result: the child adds marks to at least 6 and draws bars 6, 3 and 2. Why line: "The biggest number is 6, so the line must go up to 6 or more." Help: guided; names are placed.
- Activity 3 (independent). Goal line: "One bar does not match the table. Fix it." Goal chip: "Fix the bar". Setup: table Eating 2, Studying 4, Playing 5; the graph shows bars 2, 4 and 6. Guess: the child taps the bar they think is wrong; the table's number appears beside its top. Result: the child drags the playing knob from 6 down to 5. Why line: "The table says playing 5, but the bar went up to 6. Now the bar is at 5." A right bar tapped shows "Eating: the table says 2 and the bar is at 2. This bar is right. Look at the others." Help: independent.
- Activity 4 (independent). Goal line: "Show each strip as a bar. Read its length in cm." Goal chip: "Strips: 0 of 3". Setup: three strips marked 7 cm, 5 cm and 3 cm (practice values), places named A, B, C. Guess: "Which strip will be the tallest bar?" The child drags each strip to a place and pulls its top to its length, then taps the longest and the shortest bar. Result: bars at 7, 5 and 3. Why line: "The longest strip is 7 cm and the shortest is 3 cm. 7 − 3 = 4 cm longer." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 1 (independent), in two steps with the book's words: "Record your daily routine (24 hours) in hours and minutes, as necessary. Note the time spent on activities like sleeping, studying, playing, eating, and others." then "Make a bar graph of the time you spend on different activities in the space given below." Goal chip: "Hours left: 24". Step 1: the table rows are Sleeping, Time in school, Studying, Eating, Playing, Other activities; the child sets the hours with plus and minus; a small note says "Use whole hours." Guess: before recording, the child taps the activity that will take the most hours. Step 2: the six names are on the base and the child drags each knob to its row's number. Result (sample day 9, 5, 2, 2, 3, 3): bars at those heights. Why line: "9 + 5 + 2 + 2 + 3 + 3 = 24. Your hours add up to 24. A day has 24 hours." The tool says "You guessed Playing. The tallest bar is Sleeping, 9 hours." when they differ. The numbers are the child's own; the sample is only a sample.
- Star Challenge 2 (independent). Goal chip: "Strips: 0 of 5". The base has five places: Mine, Friend 1, Friend 2, Friend 3, Friend 4. A pinned task note holds the book's words: "Cut long paper strips from waste paper. Give one strip (each of the same width) to each of your friends. Now, put the paper strip on your index finger and tear off the extra strip extending above your fingers." The instruction line: "Paste these paper strips along the horizontal line in the given bar graph." Guess: the child taps whose finger will be the longest. The child pulls each of the five strips to the measured length. Then four cards in the book's words: "Whose index finger is the longest? ___" (tap a bar), "The length of the longest index finger is ___ cm." (number pad), "The smallest index finger is ___ cm long." (number pad), "It belongs to ___." (tap a name). Result with the sample strips: "The tops are at 6, 7, 5, 8 and 6. Friend 3 reaches 8, the highest, so the longest index finger is Friend 3's, 8 cm. The lowest top is 5, so the smallest is 5 cm and it belongs to Friend 2." Answers follow the child's own strips; with two equal tallest strips either name is right.
5. Mathematical Understanding
- Building shows the steps: names on the base, a vertical line that reaches at least the biggest number, each bar up to its number, then a check against the table or the total of 24.
- A bar can be a real length: the tallest bar is the longest strip, the lowest is the shortest, and the gap is how much longer.
- Rules: "Write the names on the base and draw each bar up to its number." "The vertical line must reach at least the biggest number."
6. Feedback and Hints
- Correct: the bar settles with a small bounce, the tag and the goal chip turn green, one line with the numbers. Every wrong answer: red strip, a small shake, ONE friendly line, free retry.
- Mistake: bar at the wrong mark -> "The table says Sleeping 7, but the bar goes up to 8. Drag the top down to 7." The top pulses.
- Mistake: line too short -> "The playing bar needs 6, but the line stops at 4. Make the line longer."
- Mistake: hours do not add up -> "Your hours add up to 22. A day has 24 hours. 2 hours are still free." With no hours left, plus says "No hours are left. Take an hour from another row first."
- Mistake: strip at the wrong cm -> "This strip is 7 cm, but its top is at 6 on the ruler."
- Mistake: wrong bar for a finger card -> "Look again. The longest index finger is the tallest bar." Wrong length -> "Look at the top of that bar. Where does it meet the ruler?"
- Mistake: width used as the number -> "All the bars and strips have the same width. Only the height tells the number or the length."
- Hints: (1) "Which number goes with this name? Look at the table." (2) a dotted line runs from the table's number to its mark on the vertical line (3) the bar rises to one mark below its number and the child finishes it.
- Edge cases: a row with 0 hours shows no bar and its name stays on the base; a strip is at least 1 cm; two equal tallest strips show "Two strips are equally tall. Tap either one."
7. Ending
- Star Challenges 1 and 2 above. Success: hours add up to 24 and all six bars match the table; five strips are set and the four finger cards are answered.
- End screen: "Well done!" Remember: "Write the names on the base and draw each bar up to its number." "The vertical line must reach at least the biggest number." "A day has 24 hours, so the hours must add up to 24." Think and talk: "How could you use your bar graph to tell a friend about your day?" Button: "Start again". A small confetti burst plays here only.
8. Assets and Language
- Images: wooden drawing board with graph paper (photo); pencil and ruler cut-outs; paper name tags; coloured paper strips of one width; round knobs; cm marks by code. English.

tool_config.idea: Make a bar graph from a table of numbers, with the names on the horizontal base and a bar up to each number on the vertical line, and make bars of real lengths in cm. The student types their own numbers and measured lengths, and the tool checks the total and the heights.
tool_config.title: Bar Graph Builder
tool_config.screen: The graph wall of Samaira and Kabir's class newsroom, drawn as a warm, polished educational-game scene with soft shadows and gentle animation, in soft cream and blue-grey wall tones. A blank graph sheet like the one in your maths book is the largest thing on screen, in the middle: the vertical line has equal marks labelled 0, 1, 2 and so on up to 10 and is called Number of Hours (Length in cm in the Lengths view), and the horizontal base has six places for names and is called Activities. A table sits beside the graph with one row for each name and a number box on each row. A view switch at the top of the wall has two settings: Table, with the table of activities and numbers, and Lengths, with a strip rack beside the sheet holding paper strips of one width and a cm ruler along the vertical line with 1 cm marked at the foot. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type, with progress dots under it. Controls: tap a number box and type a number, or use the small minus and plus steppers to change it by 1, and the bar of that row grows or shrinks at once; on the first card only, tap a row to light up its bar and tap a bar to light up its row; tap a place on the base and type a name, or tap one of the small name tags that the table offers; drag the top of a bar up or down to a mark, and it snaps to the nearest whole mark; in the Lengths view drag a paper strip from the rack to its place on the base and drag its top to the length the student measured, which is typed or stepped in cm; Check; Hint; Undo, which takes back the last change; Retry, which clears the bars of this step; Reset, which clears the table and the sheet; Back and Next in the same places on every card. The cutting and tearing of real paper strips is hands-on and stays outside the tool: the student measures their real strip with a ruler and types the length. Read-outs: a Total read-out under the table that adds all the numbers and, in the 24-hour challenge, compares the sum with 24, a small height tag that shows the number at the top of the bar being moved, a Longest and a Shortest read-out in the Lengths view, and a card number out of 7. Every bar and strip has the same width. The bars are one friendly colour, in the warm colour of Sheela's bars, the bar or number being asked about glows bright tangerine, a right answer turns green, and a look again note is soft amber, never red.
feedback: When a number is typed the bar grows to it and the tool says so, for example: Sleeping is 7 hours, so the bar goes up to 7.

The Total read-out adds the numbers. In the 24-hour challenge, if the sum is not 24 a soft amber note says, for example: Your hours add up to 22. A day has 24 hours. When the sum is 24 it says: Your hours add up to 24. A day has 24 hours. Well done.
If a bar is higher or lower than its number, a soft amber note says, for example: Look again. The sleeping bar reaches 8, but the table says 7. Drag the top down to 7.
If a number is bigger than the top mark of the sheet, the tool says: This number is bigger than the top mark, 10. Check the number you typed.

In the Lengths view a strip dragged to the right length says: The strip is 7 cm long, so its top meets 7 on the vertical line. If its top is at the wrong mark, a soft amber note says: Look again. The ruler shows 5 cm for this strip, but its top is at 6.
All bars and strips have the same width, and the tool says so: Only the height tells the number or the length, so a wider bar would not be a bigger number.
In the Lengths view the Longest and Shortest read-outs name the strips, for example: Longest: Friend 3, 8 cm. Shortest: Friend 2, 5 cm.
tool_config.done_when: The student has built the bar graph of the three practice numbers, found and fixed the bar that was too tall, shown the three practice strips as bars and named the longest and the shortest, and then made a bar graph of their own 24 hours and of their five measured finger lengths and answered the four finger questions.

media.context: Concept image for Making a Bar Graph. It follows the idea of the book's bar graph of a day (the vertical line, the horizontal base and the bars) and uses the numbers of this concept's own example: sleeping 8, school 6, studying 3, playing 4 and other 3 hours.
media.composition: One bar graph: the vertical line marked 0 to 9 and called Number of Hours, the horizontal base called Activities with five names, and five amber bars of equal width.

media.teaching_notes: Predict first: Samaira tears paper strips as long as three pencils, 9 cm, 6 cm and 4 cm, and stands them side by side on a graph. Which strip is the longest, and how much longer is it than the shortest? On this graph the vertical line is a ruler. It has 1 cm at the foot, then 2 cm, 3 cm and so on. The height of a bar is the length in cm. In your maths book you lay a paper strip on a finger, tear off the extra, and paste the strip on the graph. All the strips have the same width, so only the height tells the length. The longest strip is the tallest bar and the shortest strip is the shortest bar. To find how much longer, take the smaller height from the bigger height. Rule: the height of a bar is the length in cm, the tallest bar is the longest, and the difference of two heights is how much longer. 1. Mark the vertical line in cm: 1 cm at the foot, then 2, 3 and so on up to 10. 2. Make one strip for each pencil, all of the same width: 9 cm, 6 cm and 4 cm long. Stand them side by side on the horizontal base. 3. Read the heights where the tops meet the vertical line: 9, 6 and 4. 4. The tallest bar is 9 cm, so the longest pencil is 9 cm. The shortest bar is 4 cm. 5. How much longer? 9 − 4 = 5 cm longer. 6. Check: the shortest, 4 cm, and 5 cm more make the longest, because 4 + 5 = 9. Answer: Longest 9 cm and shortest 4 cm. The longest is 9 − 4 = 5 cm longer

content.text:
1. Predict first: Samaira tears paper strips as long as three pencils, 9 cm, 6 cm and 4 cm, and stands them side by side on a graph. Which strip is the longest, and how much longer is it than the shortest?
2. On this graph the vertical line is a ruler. It has 1 cm at the foot, then 2 cm, 3 cm and so on. The height of a bar is the length in cm.
3. In your maths book you lay a paper strip on a finger, tear off the extra, and paste the strip on the graph. All the strips have the same width, so only the height tells the length.
4. The longest strip is the tallest bar and the shortest strip is the shortest bar.
5. To find how much longer, take the smaller height from the bigger height.
6. Rule: the height of a bar is the length in cm, the tallest bar is the longest, and the difference of two heights is how much longer.

content.text:
Worked example: Samaira measures three pencils: 9 cm, 6 cm and 4 cm (practice values). Show them as bars on a graph marked in cm. Which pencil is the longest and which is the shortest? How much longer is the longest than the shortest?
{{DIAGRAM:M2.S10.T10.C52.IMG2}}
1. Mark the vertical line in cm: 1 cm at the foot, then 2, 3 and so on up to 10.
2. Make one strip for each pencil, all of the same width: 9 cm, 6 cm and 4 cm long. Stand them side by side on the horizontal base.
3. Read the heights where the tops meet the vertical line: 9, 6 and 4.
4. The tallest bar is 9 cm, so the longest pencil is 9 cm. The shortest bar is 4 cm.
5. How much longer? 9 − 4 = 5 cm longer.
6. Check: the shortest, 4 cm, and 5 cm more make the longest, because 4 + 5 = 9.
Answer: Longest 9 cm and shortest 4 cm. The longest is 9 − 4 = 5 cm longer

content.text:
{{DIAGRAM:M2.S12.T12.C59.IMG1}}
1. This is a hands-on activity. The sample below uses practice values, and your friends' strips will differ.
2. Cut five long strips of the same width, one for you and one for each of four friends.
3. Lay a strip on an index finger and tear off the extra part. Do this for each of the five fingers.
4. The sample strips are: Mine $6\text{ cm}$, Friend $1$ with $7\text{ cm}$, Friend $2$ with $5\text{ cm}$, Friend $3$ with $8\text{ cm}$ and Friend $4$ with $6\text{ cm}$.
[Image: Whose Index Finger is Longer?: Ans1: solution]
5. Paste each strip standing up from the horizontal base, in its own place: Mine, then Friend $1$ to Friend $4$. The vertical line has $1\text{ cm}$ marked at the foot, so the top of a strip tells how long the strip is.
6. Check: the top of each strip meets its length on the vertical line, $6$, $7$, $5$, $8$ and $6$.
Answer: Sample answer (practice values): strips of $6$, $7$, $5$, $8$ and $6\text{ cm}$ for Mine and Friend $1$ to $4$. Your answer will differ.
[Image: Whose Index Finger is Longer?: Ans1: solution (continued)]

5. To say which day had less, compare two bars. Monday's bar is 3 and Thursday's bar is 5, so Monday had less than Thursday.
